strengths: Comprehensive and convincing experimental evaluation: results span image models (SD3, FLUX.1-dev), video (CogVideoX-2B), real-image editing, and instruction-based editing models (Step1X-Edit, FLUX.1 Kontext dev), with both training-free and commercial baselines

A new 300-pair benchmark (ColorCtrl-Bench) plus supplementary metrics (Y-GCS, Y-GMS, VIEScore-based SC/PQ, user study) mitigate the known weaknesses of CLIP-similarity evaluation and support the central claims
Well-executed ablations (structure preservation, color preservation, mask threshold sensitivity) and honest failure-case analysis increase credibility of results
Practically useful properties: no per-layer/timestep hand-tuning, word-level attribute re-weighting that is new for MM-DiT, and demonstrated downstream value (fine-tuning data generation)
Clear writing and a well-organized method decomposition relating each attention quadrant (vision-to-vision, vision-to-text, text-to-vision) to a specific editing function
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: the main components are direct adaptations of established U-Net-era techniques (prompt-to-prompt attention swapping, PnP-style value injection, P2P attention re-weighting) to the MM-DiT architecture; the conceptual contribution is an architecture transplant rather than a fundamentally new mechanism

The rendering-theoretic formulation (Eqs. 1-2, constraints C1-C3) is largely decorative; the method does not actually estimate or enforce these physical scene parameters, so claims of 'film industry-level' physically consistent editing are stronger than what is demonstrated

Potential evaluation bias toward the proposed approach: the main benchmark uses a noise-to-image setting (not real-image inversion), and consistency metrics (PSNR/SSIM on background, Canny-SSIM) inherently favor a method whose mechanism copies source attention/value tokens; lower CLIP similarity vs. commercial models is explained away qualitatively

Baselines were reimplemented and hyperparameter-tuned by the authors, and GPT-4o is used both as a competitor and as the LLM judge for SC/PQ scores, raising fairness/conflict-of-interest concerns; results from limited-baseline user study (only 34 cases, 24 raters) are supportive but small-scale

Dependence on prompt-based mask extraction is a known failure mode (acknowledged in Fig. 16), and extension to real images relies on external inversion, so the strongest claims apply mainly to synthetic/noise-to-image settings

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: results across SD3, FLUX.1-dev, CogVideoX, Step1X-Edit, and FLUX.1 Kontext dev, on both PIE-Bench and a new 300-pair benchmark (ColorCtrl-Bench), plus ablations, a mask-threshold sensitivity study, and a blinded user study (64.7% preference).

The method is simple and practical: structure preservation via attention-map swap plus value-token copying outside the extracted mask, applied uniformly across all layers and timesteps, requiring essentially no manual hyperparameter tuning - a genuine usability advantage over baselines like DiTCtrl/FireFlow/RF-Solver that need layer/timestep selection.

The use of vision-to-text attention quadrants for mask extraction (rather than averaging vision-to-text and text-to-vision) is a sensible MM-DiT-specific insight, supported by Fig. 3(b), and the ablation (Tab. 4) cleanly shows each component's contribution.

Benchmark protocol details are disclosed and mostly fair: fixed seeds, fixed sampler, hyperparameter tuning documented for reimplemented baselines, and supplementary gradient-based (Y-GCS, Y-GMS) and VIEScore (SC, PQ) metrics added beyond CLIP similarity.
Extension to video editing and to instruction-based editing models (second-round editing refinement) is a nice breadth demonstration, and the fine-tuning application in B.1 shows downstream utility.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate/incremental. The method is a combination of well-known components: prompt-to-prompt style source/target branches with attention-map swapping (Hertz et al., Cao et al.), attention-based mask extraction (Cai et al.), and value-token injection (MasaCtrl/PnP lineage), adapted to MM-DiT. The adaptation is sensible but the conceptual contribution is limited.

The headline consistency numbers are partly an artifact of the protocol. The main benchmarks use a noise-to-image setting (no inversion), so 'consistency' largely reflects re-generation with a fixed seed rather than editing of real images; real-image results (Tab. 12) are relegated to the appendix and show a much smaller margin. Methods that edit less aggressively will trivially win BG-preservation/Canny-SSIM metrics.

There is an unresolved tension in the results: the method's edited-region CLIP similarity is the lowest among most baselines (e.g., 26.96 vs 27.54 fix-seed on SD3), which is explained away as commercial models producing 'over-saturated' edits. The SC/PQ scores from a GPT-4o evaluator are used to support this, but the evaluator is the same model family as one of the compared commercial baselines, and no human study covers the commercial comparisons directly at scale (24 raters, 34 cases).

Claims of 'surpassing GPT-4o Image Generation and FLUX.1 Kontext Max' are overstated given the above: the comparison favors a training-free method optimized for preservation metrics on synthetic source images rather than a general editing capability comparison.

Baselines were reimplemented by the authors with tuned hyperparameters (some admittedly constrained by artifacts, e.g., FireFlow/RF-Solver timestep restrictions on SD3), which introduces potential for unintentional handicapping; no external reproduction is provided.

The task formulation in Sec. 3.1 (rendering decomposition into G, L, A, S, C) is motivational dressing; the method never enforces or measures these physical constraints directly, so claims about 'physically consistent' and 'light-matter interaction' editing rest on qualitative examples.
Code is only promised upon acceptance, limiting immediate reproducibility of the benchmark and reimplemented baselines.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper defines text-guided color editing via rendering factors (geometry, illumination, albedo, material) with explicit constraints (C1)-(C3), which crisply scopes the task and the evaluation.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: comparisons against six training-free baselines and two commercial models (FLUX.1 Kontext Max, GPT-4o) on two image models (SD3, FLUX.1-dev), a video model (CogVideoX-2B), and instruction-based editors (Step1X-Edit, FLUX.1 Kontext dev), plus a new 300-prompt benchmark, ablations, a user study, and additional gradient-based and VIEScore-style metrics in the appendix.

Strong, consistent quantitative gains: the method dominates baselines on Canny-SSIM, BG preservation (PSNR/SSIM), and Y-GCS/Y-GMS across both benchmarks and modalities, with ablations (Table 4) cleanly attributing gains to structure preservation and color preservation.

Practically appealing properties: training-free, model-agnostic, works across all attention layers and timesteps without hand-tuned layer/timestep selection (unlike DiTCtrl, FireFlow, RF-Solver), and the re-weighting mechanism is a sensible MM-DiT-specific adaptation given the inapplicability of CLIP-embedding or cross-attention scaling.

The analysis distinguishing the roles of the four attention quadrants (vision-to-vision for structure, vision-to-text for masking, text-to-vision for re-weighting) and the ablation on swapping text-to-text parts / V^text is insightful and supports the design choices.
Good qualitative results showing physically consistent edits (reflections, specular highlights, droplets) and honest failure-case discussion plus a clear limitations section.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core ingredients are adaptations of established techniques—attention-map swapping from the source branch (Prompt-to-Prompt, MasaCtrl), attention-based mask extraction, and value-token replacement—to MM-DiT. The contribution is more engineering/systematization than a fundamentally new mechanism, and the paper could better acknowledge and dissect this incremental nature.

The headline quantitative comparisons are largely in a noise-to-image setting on prompts whose source images are generated by the same model family; this is favorable to self-attention-transfer methods. Real-image editing (which requires inversion) is relegated to the appendix and shows much smaller margins (Table 12), so claims of superiority should be tempered accordingly.

The new ColorCtrl-Bench is generated by GPT from a simple template (Fig. 23) with single-object, unambiguous color edits—exactly the regime the method is designed for—raising potential benchmark-author bias; there is no independent validation of the benchmark's difficulty or diversity.

Potential metric circularity: the method copies value tokens from the source in non-edited regions, so extremely high BG-preservation PSNR/SSIM is partly by construction; the paper argues CLIP similarity penalizes commercial models for 'realism,' but this claim rests on qualitative judgments and a small user study (24 participants) rather than stronger perceptual evidence.

Some inconsistencies and minor issues: the 'rendering function' formalism (Eq. 1-2) is decorative and never operationalized; 'state-of-the-art' claims are restricted to MM-DiT training-free methods in places but stated more broadly elsewhere; occasional typos ('as shwon', 'a orange fox').

Comparison fairness concerns: several baselines required reimplementation with custom timestep/block restrictions (Appendix A.3), and FireFlow is omitted on SD3 'due to worse consistency than fixed seeds'—while justified, this weakens the completeness of the comparison.

The attribute re-weighting module is evaluated only qualitatively (Fig. 5) with no quantitative protocol, and the claim that it 'violates the assumption that attention scores should sum to one' in DiTCtrl is asserted rather than demonstrated.
